title: `http_client` enhancement: pagination
bodyText:
(copied from #20844 )
I'm dealing with this one again with yet another API so I want to revive this discussion
I don't know what the correct general way to handle pagination is, since every API is going to be different. Okta handles it with a Link header, Kandji handles it with a next link in the payload, Slack handles it with response_metadata.next_cursor in the payload
I think that maybe one solution is to add a pagination section to the http_client source and allow the user to write VRL that will generate the next URL to fetch (or null to reset to whatever the original URL is?)
For something like the Okta streaming API (just as an example. I've written the Okta source to handle this specific case) the API always returns a rel=next link, and the client is meant to pause when the payload is empty but continue processing with that next link (or, in other words, the URL to process next cycle is updated rather than reset.) I suppose something like a reset_after_pagination option or some such?
The issues here I guess is how to expose a state machine to VRL (what indicates that it should stop?) and the internal configuration (ie, the url that it should hit next time)
I'm happy to actually make the change myself, and write an RFC around it but I'd like to hear from others first

title: Source idea: HTTP API collector for Fastly Signal Science
bodyText:
I've been playing with the idea of using Vector to try and pull log data from Fastly Signal Science solution using their API. https://docs.fastly.com/en/ngwaf/extract-your-data
It seems that the HTTP Client source would be a good base for this but their API throws up some interesting issues to solve.
Firstly, the responses are paginated so it would need to be aware of that and look for the next page URL given in the response and automatically fetch that, eventually getting all the pages for the full data set. So I guess the the source would be making multiple HTTP requests to the API as needed.
Also the from/until timestamp - as these require UTC timestamp values they'd need to be dynamic and based on the current time that the source collection start. I was thinking about having it expressed as an negative offset from "now" in minutes. i.e from = now-10m, until = now-5m then run the source with a 5m interval. I was also thinking if now should be aligned to the nearest 5 minute to account for any delay from the desired start time and the actual time.
So yeah, I don't think this is possible out-of-the box and requires modifying the default HTTP Client source but I'd love some feed back on possible approaches or gotchas.

title: Alerts on vector metrics
bodyText:
Hello, community! I have a question regarding internal vector metrics.
There are cases when:

Vector stops collecting logs from Kubernetes.
Vector cannot send logs because a sink
2.1.  is unavailable.
2.2. blocked by a rate limiter.

The solution for 2.2 seems pretty straightforward. I came up with the following promql.
rate(vector_events_discarded_total[2m]) > 0

For the 2.1, it is possible to alert if there are no out events for the sink.
rate(vector_events_out_total{component_kind="sink"}[2m]) == 0

Yet it needs to be more accurate because the real problem is when the end of a sink responds with errors, but I need help finding a generic approach.
No idea how to alert on 1. There are many metrics, and it is not clear to me which one to pick.
I'd appreciate it if someone could take a look at what I'm doing and give me some hints hot to setup alerting rules correctly for vector.

title: Vector crashes on k8s if the sink goes down
bodyText:
I'm in a bit of a pickle. I'm running vector as an aggregator on k8s, configured to consume data from a http server source and push to an Elasticsearch sink.
After running a few tests, it looks like if the sink goes down, but data is still flowing in, Vector pods will eventually crash and show the following error:
The container last terminated with exit code 137 because of OOMKilled.


I've found the following related issues:

#11942
#17942
#18578 - similar; points to a bug in vector that was resolved, but for a different sink
#19815 - sounds similar to what we're experiencing

But I'm a bit confused about it. Mainly because as soon as the sink goes down, the sources will start seeing non-200 http status codes, which to me feels like the the buffering mechanism does not work or it's not intended to work in this case. If it would, I should see 200 since the request made it through to vector and should only start returning non-200 after the buffer is full and can no longer take anymore data.
I'm just looking for some clarification on what exactly is the expected behaviour:

Does vector buffer events send to the http endpoint?
If requests return non-200, does this mean that the events were still buffered? The non-200 just means that we didn't get an ack from vector/sink that the events made it through?
Is there some documentation on the status codes returned from vector when using the http source? At first, it looked like the status codes are the same as Elasticsearch returned, but that cannot be true since there may be multiple sinks returning different status codes

I use the vector helm chart with the following config:

  role: "Aggregator"

  image:
    repository: timberio/vector
    pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    tag: "0.42.0-alpine"

  replicas: 2

    - name: ES_USERNAME

    - name: ES_PASSWORD

        secretKeyRef:
          name: elastic-user
          key: elastic

  resources: {}

  persistence:
    enabled: true

  # NOTE: When we set this, we need to configure a bunch of other stuff (e.g. HAProxy, etc.)
  # https://github.com/vectordotdev/helm-charts/blob/develop/charts/vector/templates/configmap.yaml
  customConfig:
    data_dir: /vector-data-dir
    api:
      enabled: true
      address: 127.0.0.1:8686
      playground: false
    acknowledgements:
      enabled: true
    # https://vector.dev/blog/log-namespacing/
    schema:
      log_namespace: true
    sources:
      # https://vector.dev/docs/reference/configuration/sources/internal_metrics/
      internal_metrics:
        type: internal_metrics
      # https://vector.dev/docs/reference/configuration/sources/host_metrics/
      host_metrics:
        type: host_metrics
      # https://vector.dev/docs/reference/configuration/sources/vector/
      vector:
        address: 0.0.0.0:6000
        type: vector
        version: "2"
      vector_http:
        type: http_server
        address: 0.0.0.0:8888
        encoding: ndjson
        method: POST
        response_code: 200
    transforms:
      logs:
        type: filter
        inputs:
          - vector_http
        condition: '.kind == "Log"'
      remapped_logs:
        type: remap
        inputs:
          - logs
        source: |-
          .@timestamp = del(.timestamp)
          .metadata = {}
          .data_stream = {}
          .data_stream.type = "logs"
          .data_stream.dataset = "blackhole"
          .data_stream.namespace = "device"
      resource_usage:
        type: filter
        inputs:
          - vector_http
        condition: '.kind == "ResourceUsage"'
      remapped_resource_usage:
        type: remap
        inputs:
          - resource_usage
        source: |-

          .data_stream = {}
          .data_stream.type = "metrics"

          .data_stream.namespace = "device"
    sinks:

        address: 0.0.0.0:9090

        inputs: [vector, vector_http]
        encoding:
          codec: json
      es_data_stream:
        type: elasticsearch
        inputs: [remapped_logs, remapped_resource_usage]
        # NOTE: We do not need to remap `timestamp` -> `@timestamp`; Vector does this for us when using `data_stream` mode.
        # https://github.com/vectordotdev/vector/blob/d49cf33748ad82292198888687b6b50a01d8500f/src/sinks/elasticsearch/mod.rs#L73
        # TODO: It seems that the above assumption is incorrect! Because w/o adding the `@timestamp`, we see:
        # 2025-02-12T05:53:22.008701Z ERROR sink{component_kind="sink" component_id=es_data_stream component_type=elasticsearch}:request{request_id=2769}: vector::sinks::util::retries: Not retriable; dropping the request. reason="error type: document_parsing_exception, reason: [1:381] failed to parse: data stream timestamp field [@timestamp] is missing" internal_log_rate_limit=true

        data_stream:

          password: "${ES_PASSWORD}"
          strategy: "basic"
        endpoints:

    # https://github.com/vectordotdev/helm-charts/blob/develop/charts/vector/templates/service.yaml
    # https://github.com/vectordotdev/helm-charts/blob/develop/charts/vector/templates/service-headless.yaml

        protocol: TCP

        protocol: TCP

        protocol: TCP
      - name: prom-exporter
        containerPort: 9090
        protocol: TCP

    service:
      annotations:
      ports:
        - name: vector
          port: 6000
          protocol: TCP
        - name: vector-http
          port: 8888
          protocol: TCP
        - name: prom-exporter
          port: 9090
          protocol: TCP

    # https://github.com/vectordotdev/helm-charts/blob/develop/charts/vector/templates/haproxy/configmap.yaml
    customConfig: |
      global
        log stdout format raw local0 debug
        maxconn 4096
        stats socket /tmp/haproxy
        hard-stop-after {{ .Values.haproxy.terminationGracePeriodSeconds }}s

      defaults
        log     global
        option  dontlognull
        retries 3
        option  redispatch
        option  allbackups
        timeout client 15s
        timeout server 15s
        timeout connect 15s

      resolvers coredns
        nameserver dns1 kube-dns.kube-system.svc.cluster.local:53
        resolve_retries 3
        timeout resolve 2s
        timeout retry 1s
        accepted_payload_size 8192
        hold valid 10s
        hold obsolete 60s

      frontend stats
        mode http
        bind :::1024
        option httplog
        http-request use-service prometheus-exporter if { path /metrics }

      frontend vector
        mode http
        bind :::6000 proto h2
        option httplog
        default_backend vector

      frontend vector_http
        mode http
        bind :::8888 proto h1
        option httplog
        default_backend vector_http

      backend vector
        mode http
        balance roundrobin
        option tcp-check
        server-template srv 10 _vector._tcp.{{ include "vector.fullname" $ }}-headless.{{ $.Release.Namespace }}.svc.cluster.local resolvers coredns proto h2 check

      backend vector_http
        mode http
        balance roundrobin
        option tcp-check
        server-template srv 10 _vector-http._tcp.{{ include "vector.fullname" $ }}-headless.{{ $.Release.Namespace }}.svc.cluster.local resolvers coredns proto h1 check

  # Direct trafic to Traefik's vector entrypoint
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    annotations:
      traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.entrypoints: vectorhttp
    hosts:
      - paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            port:
              name: vector-http

NOTE: On the source side, we have agents pushing to the http endpoint. As soon as a non-200 occurs, they will stop sending new events and keep retrying (at the first failure) until it receives 200, then it continues pushing. There's also a buffering mechanism on the agent side.

title: Vector not accepting connections on sink failure
bodyText:
I'm using Vector v0.35.0 in an aggregator configuration, where it accepts json via HTTP, from FluentBit agents, and inserting it into ClickHouse using the sink. I'm hosting it on AWS ECS Fargate in front of an NLB with health-checks enabled based on the API /health endpoint.
Whenever the sink starts to experience a large amount of failures, in my case a number of "connection resets" from ClickHouse Cloud whenever it scales up, Vector will soon stop accepting connections resulting in an unhealthy task and being killed off by AWS. Vector also shoots up in memory, but there's nothing indicating in the logs (level=info) to indicate that.
I tried buffering to filesystem to see how it would perform and it resulted in a 2-3x performance decrease, which is a considerable amount at our scale, so I haven't tried that out with ClickHouse Cloud scaling up.
Example error:
2024-02-06T08:57:49.515492Z  WARN sink{component_kind="sink" component_id=clickhouse_envoy component_type=clickhouse}:request{request_id=9069}:http: vector::internal_events::http_client: HTTP error. error=connection closed before message completed error_type="request_failed" stage="processing" internal_log_rate_limit=true

Vector config:
api:
  enabled: true
  address: "0.0.0.0:8686" 

sources:
  envoy_in:
    type: http_server
    address: 0.0.0.0:8123

    path_key: __vector_http_path

title: Confused about "{{ host }}" and the template syntax in config files
bodyText:
Question
Early on in my use of vector I wrote a toml configuration using "{{ host }}" in my sink definitions to specify per-host log destinations. Here is one of several sinks I have:
[sinks.axiom-webapp]

Now despite quite a bit of searching I cannot find the documentation that describes "{{ host }}" as a mechanism. Neither https://vector.dev/docs/reference/configuration/ nor https://vector.dev/docs/reference/configuration/template-syntax/ mention it. I must have read it somewhere though, and it does work.
Interestingly, I asked Claude to read the docs and it thinks that "the {{ }} syntax is exclusively for referencing event data fields at runtime, not arbitrary config variables." This is clearly not strictly true because the above config is working.
I am curious what the dev team's take is.
I would love to see some documentation describing the complete list of "global" variables (or whatever you call them; I mean the variables that aren't event fields) that are available in the template syntax. I am also interested to know if using the template syntax in configs is recommended, given that the documentation is confusing in this department.
I'd be happy to file an issues describing more specifically where I think the docs fall short. The team has been fantastically receptive to those issues in the past and I appreciate it. I didn't do so in this case because I don't want it to seem like I'm using docs issues just to ask for help.

title: Unexpected re-processing of old log files (30h+) after OOM crash despite ignore_older_secs: 86400 and successful S3 delivery
bodyText:
Question
Hi Vector team,
I am experiencing an unexpected behavior where Vector re-processes and re-uploads old log files to S3 after a pod crash, even though those files were successfully uploaded hours before the crash and should have been filtered out by ignore_older_secs.
Environment:
Platform: EKS (Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service)
Vector Version: 0.53.0
Vector Role: Log collector (Agent)
Source: file
Sink: aws_s3
Timezone: KST (UTC+9)
Incident Timeline (KST):
Mar 16, 09:00 - 16:00: Vector was running normally. Logs from the morning (Mar 16 AM) were successfully read and uploaded to S3.
Mar 16, 16:00: The EKS node and Vector pod crashed (OOM Killed).
Mar 17, 17:00: The pod was finally restored after increasing memory limits.
Observation: Upon restoration, Vector re-read and re-uploaded Mar 16 AM logs (approx. 31 hours old at the time of restoration) from the beginning, causing significant duplicates in S3/Databricks.
The Mystery:
At the time of restoration (Mar 17, 17:00 KST), the files from Mar 16, 09:41 KST were 31+ hours old.
Why did the file source pick up these files despite ignore_older_secs: 86400?
If the files were successfully uploaded before the crash, why did Vector lose the checkpoint or decide to re-read from the beginning (position: 0)?
I suspect this might be related to Issue #17208, where checkpoints are expired if they are older than ignore_older_secs during startup. However, I don't understand why these files bypassed the "discovery" filter in the first place if they were already older than 24 hours.
Could you help me understand why Vector ignores the 24h filter for these specific files and why the previous checkpoints were not honored or were deleted?

title: AWS MSK (Kafka) Support
bodyText:
Hello,
I have seen several issues related to AWS's MSK support not being fully supported or tested. References: #1516 and #1833
I have considered contributing to this, but I wanted to check in to see what the maintainers would prefer to implement it.
tl;dr AWS has some nuances with Authenticating to their managed Kafka product; they have created a library/reference implementation that is available at https://github.com/aws/aws-msk-iam-auth/tree/main, and there are Rust implementations available too https://github.com/yuhao-su/aws-msk-iam-sasl-signer-rs/tree/main
Most of the Rust implementation's functionality already exists within the vector codebase, so I don't see it as useful to implement by pulling in yet another dependency. I would be keen to get a maintainer's thoughts on this, just in case I am off track.
Implementation Idea
IAMS support leverages existing OAUTHBEARER support in rdkafka, which is handled by implementing a method generate_oauth_token, that generates and maintains the authentication credentials transparently. The existing Kafka implementation uses this purely for statistics. By updating this to include OAUTH, it could work for source and sink configurations. An example from the Rust implementation can be found here.
If the client's sasl configuration is not using OAUTHBEARER, it shouldn't be used, so it should be a non-breaking change for existing users. What I wasn't clear about from reading the source was what the idiomatic way to refresh AWS credentials is. This would be required in the ClientContext method so that credentials continue to work as AWS expires them. The OAUTH token needs to be signed. It looks like this needs to be implemented directly; the existing functions appear to handle signing requests. Is that correct?
Now this poses some additional questions that are more vector/business logic than technical....
Introducing MSK support introduces the framework to support OAUTHBEARER support more generically when using upstream Kafka. OAUTHBEARER support is built into the library out of the box; the use cases I've tested seem to work fine with the various providers that I tested with. The credential refresh appears to work flawlessly in all cases except AWS's MSK, which would suggest that the ClientContext would only need to refresh the tokens IF it's MSK. This could be written to be extended in the future with an enum or similar to match on the type. Similar to how HTTP Auth works with strategy: Basic, ... AWS. I'm keen to understand how that would be received in a PR Do we need to implement everything OAUTH or create the foundation to be extensible in the future?
** Summary **
We would like to contribute MSK support to Vector using OAUTHBEARER and using as much of the existing codebase as possible, rather than bringing in additional dependencies and duplicated capabilities; however, we have the following questions


What's the idiomatic/preferred way to refresh AWS credentials in the ClientContext? Are there any examples of where that happens in the codebase as it stands today?


Should we aim to support extensibility in OAUTH patterns for Kafka or create a much smaller patch set that's more focused on MSK with a strong focus on superb documentation?

title: Vector Aggregator Discarding Metrics
bodyText:
Question
We have a DD Agent -> Vector Aggregator -> Datadog metrics pipeline setup. However, we have noticed that there are a lot of discarded events. It looks like all discarded events are coming from component_id: filter_histogram_metrics, component_type: filter.
We have tried tweaking the buffer.max_events, batch.max_events, and request.adaptive_concurrency parameters to see if that would help reduce discarded events, but no luck. Currently, we have only enabled vector as passthrough, as in metrics go through the remap transform, but don't satisfy the condition that removes the tags (see comments in vector config remap transform). This means that we haven't started removing tags yet, however, teams have still been reporting a loss of metrics triggering false alerts.
Can you please assist us in preventing metrics from being dropped?
Vector Discarded Events By Component ID & Component Type

Vector Received Events vs Discarded Events

Vector Config
# Configuration for the vector chart dependency
# All values under this key get passed to the vector chart v0.45.0
vector:
  # Vector configuration for Datadog agents -> Vector -> Datadog pipeline
  # For available options, see: https://github.com/vectordotdev/helm-charts/tree/develop/charts/vector

  logLevel: info

  # Using stateless aggregator to prioritize high availability (faster pod restarts) in tradeoff for some data loss, which would be minimal
  role: Stateless-Aggregator

  # Enable horizontal pod autoscaling with a minimum of 3 replicas to spread across our AZs
  # Overwriting subchart defaults so we have better control over the HPA
  # By default, HPA scale up stabilization window is 0 seconds and scale down stabilization window is 300 seconds
  # https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/
  autoscaling:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 3
    maxReplicas: 10
    targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 60

  # Tolerate public-subnets nodes
  tolerations:
    - key: nd.group-name
      effect: NoExecute
      value: public-subnets
      operator: Equal

  # Select public-subnets nodes
  nodeSelector:
    nextdoor.com/type: public
    kubernetes.io/os: linux

  # Spread pods across our AZs
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      minDomains: 3  # This ensures that we have public-subnet nodes in each of our 3 AZs
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule  # This forces Spot to spin up nodes in new zones and spread pods evenly across our AZs
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: vector

  # Setting resources for the vector pods
  # The CPU limit is not set to allow the container to use more CPU resources if needed
  # The pods will be in Burstable QOS
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 3
      memory: 4Gi
    limits:
      memory: 5Gi

  podMonitor:
    enabled: true

  podDisruptionBudget:
    enabled: true
    minAvailable: 3

  service:

    # Enable topology-aware routing
    annotations:
      service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto

    # Expose the datadog_agent port for receiving data from your Datadog agents
    ports:
    - name: datadog-agent
      port: 8282
      targetPort: 8282
      protocol: TCP

  # Custom configuration for the vector chart: https://vector.dev/docs/reference/configuration/
  customConfig:
    # Global options - required when using customConfig
    data_dir: /vector-data-dir

    # Sources - receive data from Datadog agents
    sources:
      datadog_agents:
        type: datadog_agent
        address: 0.0.0.0:8282
        multiple_outputs: true
        store_api_key: false

    # Transforms - delete unnecessary host tags (cardinality reduction)
    transforms:
      remove_host_tag:
        type: remap
        inputs:
          - datadog_agents.metrics
        source: |-

          cluster_env = "${CLUSTER_APP_ENVIRONMENT}"
          cluster_group = "${CLUSTER_APP_GROUP}"
          cluster_name = "${CLUSTER_NAME}"
          cluster_region = "${CLUSTER_REGION}"

          if cluster_env != "" {
            .tags.env = cluster_env
          }
          if cluster_group != "" {
            .tags.app_group = cluster_group
          }
          if cluster_name != "" {
            .tags.eks_cluster = cluster_name
            .tags.cluster_name = cluster_name
            .tags.cluster_id = cluster_name
          }
          if cluster_region != "" {
            .tags.region = cluster_region
          }

          # Currently, no metrics contain the remove_host_tag, so this block does not actually run
          # This was done to ensure the vector aggregator works without data loss prior to us dropping tags
          if (exists(.tags.host) && exists(.tags.remove_host_tag)) {
            host_value = .tags.host
            del(.tags.host)
            # If the metric is not a distribution, we need to set a tag for uniqueness. Use the vector host, which should have lower cardinality than the datadog host.
            if .kind != "distribution" {
              .tags.vector_host = "${HOSTNAME}"
            }
            log("Forwarding processed metrics: " + encode_json(.))

title: SQS Source wrap up
bodyText:
Question
There are many questions related to the SQS source, and since I am currently investigating SQS, I figured it was worth consolidating them into a single summary question.
At the moment, we have several very busy SQS queues, with many billions of events per day. vector is handling this with ease (awesome work to everyone who's worked on the source/sink ❤️ )
Concurrency
The existing concurrency model has some room for improvement. When the SQS queue is very busy, all of the nodes' concurrency is running well, and we may see a slight increase in the max message age. However, when the message rate is slower, the number of consumers per host remains constant. This results in the CloudWatch metric NumberOfEmptyReceives increasing. When many nodes have a high concurrency level configured, this can result in unnecessary costs and wasted compute.
I've had a look at how this is handled in other sources or sinks, and there are several approaches. The current implementation of the SQS sink uses an adaptive concurrency model that appears to be based on round-trip time. A similar approach could be used to dynamically adjust the concurrency based on the message attribute SentTimestamp, which is already being extracted in get_timestamp().
A MessageAgeMonitor would need to be implemented to dynamically track and manage concurrency. The message age thresholds could be configured in the source, with a max concurrency value that defaults to the number of cores or a configured value. An alternative to strictly configured values is to use an exponentially weighted moving average of message ages. This is probably a more user-friendly approach, but it may need a broader discussion, as there are many possible approaches.
Another common approach across sinks is the common::backoff::ExponentialBackoff crate/module/library. Implementing this would be less work; however, I wanted to reach out to discuss and see what the maintainers prefer.
Message attributes
There are many different discussions and issues that cover this; it seems to be something that isn't outright rejected and is looking for someone to implement it. While I am sure that many people overload the use of attributes, one use case that is useful is encoding the source request_id or similar application metadata in the attributes and leaving the original message intact. Sometimes this is used for routing decisions because the message doesn't need to be deserialised or parsed.
Has anyone put any time into thinking about a preferred implementation for handling message attributes? My naive thinking has been to use the dropped_fields ObjectMap in the EventMetadata, but from reading issues and comments, that might not be the right choice.
SQS DLQ
SQS supports DLQ, in the scenario where receiving messages from external "untrusted" sources is possible, messages may not be well formed, or may have become corrupted (rare). Has there been any discussion about adding DLQ support for messages that can't be processed correctly the first x times?
These are items that we are in a position to resolve through sending in a PR, particularly the concurrency item as it's currently an item showing up in our aws bills. These would be submitted as separate smaller PR's based on whatever path forward can be agreed to (or not).
Thanks in advance,
James.

title: Dynamic schema
bodyText:
Question
I'm looking at possibly using Vector to connect a message producer to a Pulsar cluster. Basically Vector would sit on the individual nodes, and handle concerns like buffering in the event of link interruption or whatnot. All the published messages follow a schema. The catch is that there are hundreds of schemas in use, and are generated dynamically, and can change. So having to manually configure Vector with all the schemas in its config is not a viable option. Vector would need to receive the schema and pass it along. Is there any way to accomplish this?
I noticed that there's a recent PR which adds OCF decoding (#24585) which would be extremely convenient, as OCF embeds the schema at the start of the stream, and would be very easy to support with the message producer we're using. But I'm unsure how that OCF decoder works, such as if it requires a configured schema still, and that the configured schema has to match the received schema.
So basically is there any way to accomplish this? Any way so that Vector can receive a schema from the source, and pass that schema along to the sink?

title: How does disk buffer cleanup work in Vector when using EFS with stateless pods
bodyText:
Hi Vector team
I’m trying to better understand how Vector disk buffers work internally, especially buffer cleanup behavior, when running Vector in Kubernetes with EFS-backed persistence and Spot instances.
Environment / Setup
Deployment type: Kubernetes Deployment
Helm role: Stateless-Aggregator
Autoscaling: Enabled (pods are ephemeral)
Node type: AWS Spot instances
Persistence: AWS EFS mounted to Vector data_dir

Purpose:
Handle frequent pod termination (Spot interruptions, rescheduling)
Avoid data loss during abrupt shutdowns
Sinks: ClickHouse
Buffer type: disk
Acknowledgements: true
Each pod uses a pod-specific data_dir to avoid concurrent writers:

Filesystem layout (inside a running pod)
df -h
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
overlay          30G  6.6G   24G  22% /
127.0.0.1:/     8.0E   92M  8.0E   1% /vector-data-dir

EFS directory structure
/vector-data-dir/
├── pod-vector-6b5d85f886-qvnm5
│   └── buffer
│       └── v2
│           ├── clickhouse_syslog
│           │   ├── buffer-data-0.dat
│           │   ├── buffer.db
│           │   └── buffer.lock
│           └── clickhouse_trafficlog
└── pod-vector-6b5d85f886-v48hb


Observed Behavior:
Data is successfully written to ClickHouse
Incoming traffic has been stopped
However:
buffer-data-0.dat .This file size dose not decreasing,.. (Does this filie store all the buffer)
Disk usage does not immediately decrease
Files remain even when there is no more traffic
Questions
1. Disk buffer lifecycle
What exactly is stored in the buffer-data-0*.dat files? Do they contain all of the buffer data?
I stopped the traffic, but the file size did not decrease. Should the file size decrease when there is no incoming traffic?
2. Handling Spot instance termination
If a pod is terminated because the Spot instance is taken away, what is the recommended way to handle unflushed buffer data?
3. Current design approach
In my current setup:
When a Spot instance is terminated, the old pod is killed.
A new pod is created.
I copy the old pod’s buffer data from:
vector-data-dir/pod-vector-${OLD_POD}/buffer/v2/<sink>

to the new pod’s directory:
vector-data-dir/pod-vector-${NEW_POD}/buffer/v2/<sink>

The idea is that the new pod will continue flushing the old pod’s buffer data.
Is this the correct approach for handling buffer persistence when using Spot instances?
Any help is very appreciated

title: Avro and Parquet enhancements
bodyText:
We have several use cases where we need to write events out as Avro- or Parquet-encoded data (e.g. to S3 and Kafka) so that downstream systems in our data platform can consume them directly.
Right now, the Avro support in Vector appears to be limited to using to_avro_datum. From the apache-avro docs:
NOTE: This function has a quite small niche of usage and does NOT generate headers and sync markers; use https://docs.rs/apache-avro/latest/apache_avro/struct.Writer.html to be fully Avro-compatible if you don’t know what you are doing, instead.

Because to_avro_datum only produces a single Avro-encoded value (no container file header, no sync markers, no codec metadata), the output isn’t directly compatible with the Avro Object Container File (OCF) format or with many “big data” tools that expect standard Avro files.
What we’d like to contribute
We’d like to improve Vector’s Avro compatibility so that it can:

Write fully compatible Avro object container files (OCF)

Use apache_avro::Writer (or an equivalent abstraction) so that:
The Avro file header is written, including:

avro.schema with the JSON schema
Sync markers are generated and written between blocks.


Target use case: writing Avro files to S3 / object storage that are consumable by Spark/Flink/other Avro tooling out of the box.
Keep the existing implementation so that it's not going to break existing users



Our goal is to make Vector’s Avro output “just work” with the broader Avro ecosystem (Java Avro, avro-tools, Spark, etc.), not only with custom consumers that know about the current to_avro_datum usage.
Proposed approach
If you’re open to this, we’d like to contribute this work as a series of small, incremental PRs that preserve existing behavior by default. Roughly:


Introduce an OCF writer path that uses apache_avro::Writer for file-style outputs, controlled via configuration (so the existing raw datum behavior can be kept for backward compatibility).


Add configuration options for:

datum (existing/default)
Avro Object Container (new)



Add compatibility tests, for example:

Golden Avro files produced by Vector that are validated with avro-tools / Java Avro.
Round-trip tests where data written by Vector is read back with the Rust apache-avro reader.



We’d really appreciate feedback on:

Whether you’d be willing to accept PRs in this direction.
Any existing design constraints we should be aware of (beyond the contributing guidelines, maybe this has been done before?).

title: Optimal way to access k8s labels having a sources type file
bodyText:
Question
Hello everyone!
I'm trying Vector as alternative for our current k8s log shipper pipeline (currently powered by Filebeat and Logstash).
I'm using the source type file instead of kubernetes_logs because I have a very heavy load on our cluster and I don't really want to stress the k8s API server to access logs, so I'm just reading them from this path /var/log/containers/*.log (at the moment as first PoC i've installed Vector as process running on a node with systemd, it's not a daemonset).
I'm getting almost everything just parsing the filename, for example:
/var/log/containers/grafana-f645ff4d7-2vqqv_minio_grafana-2455b25e0bf402fbf7cf7c5e202df3309ab4b24ae8b732ca74e4a2523bc3323f.log
I get grafana-f645ff4d7-2vqqv as pod name, minio as namespace and grafana as container name. The last part it's the container id.
Also I added a bunch of extra logic to get other fields, using some transforms type remap, which are out of scope for my post.
My question is, I have to add to my log a certain k8s Label called app.kubernetes.io/name: is it possible to get this information in some way? Like for example can I just read labels / metadata from my k8s without getting the whole log?
Of course I tried the source type kubernetes_logs (with that I indeed can access the label I want), but it adds too much overhead to be actually used in my production environment.
Thank you in advance.
Vector Config
sources:
  in:
    type: file
    include:
      - /var/log/containers/*.log
    read_from: end
    ignore_older_secs: 60
    offset_key: offset
    fingerprint:
      strategy: device_and_inode

transforms:
  extract_k8s_metadata:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - in
    source: |
      # Extract just the filename from the full path
      filename = split!(.file, "/")[-1]
      
      # Remove the .log extension
      filename = replace!(filename, r'\.log$', "")
      
      # Split by underscores
      parts = split!(filename, "_")
      
      # First part is pod_name, second is namespace
      .pod_name = parts[0]
      .namespace = parts[1]

      # 3. container_name
      # Take the third part (postfix-2955...) and remove the last hyphen + ID
      # Regex explanation:
      #   -       : match a literal hyphen
      #   [^-]+   : match one or more characters that are NOT hyphens
      #   $       : match the end of the string
      .container_name = replace!(parts[2], r'-[^-]+$', "")
      container = split!(parts[2], "-")

      #.container_name = container[0]
      .container_id = container[-1]
      
      # Set default severity level
      .level = "info"
      # Convert msg to lowercase
      mymsg = downcase(string!(.message))
      # Patterns that must remain with level info
      ignored_patterns = [
        "smtpd_client_event_limit_exceptions",
        "debug_peer_list"
      ]
      # Check if message matches any pattern set in ignored_patterns
      ignore = false
      for_each(ignored_patterns) -> |_index, pattern| {
        if contains(mymsg, pattern) {
          ignore = true
        }
      }
      # Parse message for severity level and apply if not in ignored_patterns
      if !ignore {
        if contains(mymsg, "error") || contains(mymsg, "failed") || contains(mymsg, "exception") {
          .level = "error"
        } else if contains(mymsg, "warn") {
          .level = "warn"
        } else if contains(mymsg, "crit") || contains(mymsg, "panic") || contains(mymsg, "fatal") {
          .level = "critical"
        } else if contains(mymsg, "debug") {
          .level = "debug"
        }
      }

      pod = to_string(.pod_name)
      #if err == null {
      app = pod

      ._source = {
        "host": {
          "name-pod-vector": .host
        },
        "@timestamp": format_timestamp!(.timestamp, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3fZ"),
        "logdest": "applications",
        "message": .message,
        "log": {
          "file": {
            "path": .file
          }
        },
        "agent": {
          "name": .host,
          "version": "0.52",
          "type": "vector"
        },
        "received_at": format_timestamp!(now(), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3fZ"),
        "kubernetes": {
          "pod": {
            "name": .pod_name
          },
          "node": {
            "name": .host
          },
          "namespace": .namespace,
          "container": {
            "name": .container_name
          },
          "labels": {
            "app_kubernetes_io/name": "my-hardcoded-application",
          }          
        },
        "container": {
          "id": .container_id
        },
        "service": [
          "k8s",
          "apache"
        ]
      }
      
      .pipeline = "vector-pipeline"

sinks:
  my_loki:
    type: loki
    inputs:
      - extract_k8s_metadata
    endpoint: http://loki-gateway.minio.svc.cluster.local
    path: /loki/api/v1/push
    tenant_id: dev
    encoding:
      codec: json
    labels:
      job: "kubernetes-logs"
      pipeline: "{{ pipeline }}"
    out_of_order_action: accept

title: Q&A - Possible Socket (UDP) issue on 0.46.0+?
bodyText:
Question
Vector runs in K8S as our internal log ingestor/aggregator/normalizer, service is behind a metallb LoadBalancer IP. The normalized events are sent to Kafka and beyond after normalization.
We ran into an issue when ingesting events through Socket/UDP when we upgraded from 0.43.1 to 0.51.1.
On our current load, we had around ~15-17k events per second (Vector's internal metrics for received events on component_kind="source" and Kafka metrics for the sink's topic align on the numbers), after upgrading with the same config in place, we only see ~6-8k eps in both, so pretty much a 2x drop in both Vector & Kafka metrics. From some testing, we noticed that this issue appears starting with 0.46.0.
Extra info:

We looked at the container logs, enabled debug, but couldn't pin down any useful errors/traces to create an issue.
We tested a bunch of versions (starting with 0.45.0 up to 0.53.0), everything looks good on 0.45.0, then the "issue" starts on 0.46.0 and onwards.
We stripped the config down to just the sources and sinks (only metrics).
The containers typically never reach even ~50% resource usage

We thought it could be a possible cluster/node issue at first (investigation still on-going), but switching back and forth between 0.43.1 and the later versions always produces the same results.
Have there been any changes in 0.46.0 and onwards that could have this effect? I realize the shortcomings of using UDP right now, but we don't have a choice at this time.
Could the containers be dropping packets silently, even though there is no serious load?

title: log_to_metric memory use - double what is required?
bodyText:
Question
I've got some log_to_metric transforms happening, which feed to an aggregate.  This is a 1:1 flow - straight through, no many-to-one concentrations - super-simple. The aggregate has a six hour timer.  I have "--allocation-tracing" turned on.  When I graph "vector_component_allocated_bytes" for all my components, I see the memory increasing (as expected) for the aggregation.  However, the log_to_metric that is feeing the aggregation is growing also, about three times larger!  (other pairings of log_to_metric:aggregate data in my model have ratios are 2:1 - significantly more than I would expect.)
When the aggregation "fires" and the messages are dumped (in my case, to kafka) I see the memory drop for both the aggregation and for the log_to_metric value.  However... memory use on the log_to_metric doesn't go to zero, as I would expect.  It reduces to around half.  The aggregate drops only a small amount.
Even more strange: after first six hour interval, there doesn't seem to be any memory reduction as I would expect given that there was a transmission to kafka and what should be a memory purge.  It's as if it skips the first interval for data expunging.  Subsequent intervals have a "drop" in memory use both in the log_to_metric and in the aggregate transforms.  But the first interval just is skipped.  In fact, the aggregate CLIMBS sharply at the end of the first 6 hours, which is entirely counter-intuitive.
And why does the aggregate climb in a step function, and not have the same curve (or any curve) as the log_to_metric graph?
Lastly: at the 12 hour mark, the log_to_metric memory volume does drop, but it drops to what appears on the graph to be exactly the level that it was at at the end of the first 6 hour interval. (see graph.)  It's like it's forgetting everything from the last 6 hours (or the first six hours?) only.  The aggregate memory use drops very little.
I am sure I do not understand this correctly.  My expectation would be that at the end of the 6 hour window (barring a few seconds or minutes of time spent "flushing" the data to kafka) that the memory usage for both the aggregate and the log_to_metric transformations for this data stream would drop to near zero and start over.  But that isn't the case - they remain quite large.  Why?
(why do I care? I'm doing some very large aggregations, and running out of memory, so I'm trying to find how I can save some bytes - these log_to_metric consumers are by far the largest users of memory if I'm to believe the data delivered with the allocation tracing flags enabled.)

title: Memory Enrichment Table with a 'metadata' file next to the log
bodyText:
Question
Hi, I have a use case where logs may be stored under ~/logs/$job_id/*.log, and I need to enrich it with metadata. I can add a separate metadata file of whatever format is required, e.g. atm i have it as a json. For this example lets say it lives in ~/logs/$job_id/job.json
The job_id is unique so can be used as the key in this case.
I'm not entirely sure from the docs whether this is a known pattern/if there is an example on getting it to work.
Vector Config
data_dir: "./vector-data"

sources:
  slurm_job_logs:
    type: "file"
    include: ["/home/*/slurm-logs/*/*.log"]
    read_from: "beginning"

  slurm_job_metadata:
    type: "file"
    include: ["/home/*/slurm-logs/*/job.json"]
    read_from: "beginning"

enrichment_tables:
  job_metadata:
    type: memory
    ttl: 3600
    flush_interval: 5
    inputs: ["slurm_job_metadata_cache"]
    schema:
      job_id: string

transforms:
  slurm_job_metadata_cache:
    type: "remap"
    inputs: ["slurm_job_metadata"]
    source: |
      metadata = parse_json!(.message)
      filepath = .file
      captures = parse_regex(filepath, r'^/home/[^/]+/slurm-logs/(?P<job_id>[^/]+)/job\.json$') ?? {}
      .job_id = to_string(captures.job_id)
      .metadata = metadata

  slurm_job_logs_processor:
    type: "remap"
    inputs: ["slurm_job_logs"]
    source: |
      filepath = .file
      captures = parse_regex(filepath, r'^/home/[^/]+/slurm-logs/(?P<job_id>[^/]+)/[^/]+\.log$') ?? {}
      job_id = to_string(captures.job_id)
      .job_id = job_id

      row, err = get_enrichment_table_record("job_metadata", {"job_id": job_id})
      if err == null {
        .metadata = row.metadata
      } else {
        .enrichment_error = to_string(err)
      }

sinks:
  console:
    inputs: ["slurm_job_logs_processor"]
    target: "stdout"
    type: "console"
    encoding:
      codec: "json"
      json:
        pretty: true

  # Debug: show what's being sent to the enrichment table
  metadata_debug:
    inputs: ["slurm_job_metadata_cache"]
    target: "stderr"
    type: "console"
    encoding:
      codec: "json"

title: Migrating from Discord to Github Discussions
bodyText:
Dear Vector Community,
After careful consideration, the Vector maintenance team has decided to migrate unofficial support from the ⁠support-archive channel to Github Discussions effective November 1, 2024. Please use GitHub Discussions for any questions or issues moving forward. This will help create a more searchable and accessible knowledge base, allowing others to easily find and learn from past discussions and solutions.
To help us assist you more efficiently, if you are reporting a bug, please create a new issue using this template: Bug Report Template. Providing more information, such as configuration, debug output, and bug reproduction steps will lead to faster responses. For other cases, please start a discussion here: Start a Discussion. If we identify a bug during the discussion, we can easily convert it into a bug report.
Our support policy is also available in https://vector.dev/community/#support.
TL;DR

For Vector bug reports: Bug Report
For Vector questions and help: GitHub Discussions
For VRL bug reports: Bug Report
For VRL questions and help: GitHub Discussions

Finally, we encourage the community to continue using other Discord channels to discuss Vector and VRL, share ideas, development tips, or anything else that may be interesting and helpful to the community.
Thank you for your understanding and continued support!

title: Extracting HAProxy JSON logs inside syslog/journald
bodyText:
Question
We're generating JSON formatted logs from HAProxy which will send to syslog / journald and are then collected by Vector. I'm trying to build a Vector configuration which can extract the fields from the JSON formatted log line and having difficulty.
The config so far will successfully parse the syslog and remove the syslog parts, leaving only the JSON log as a string inside a message object. But I cant figure out how to then parse that string as JSON. The final output should be only the HTTP request, status code and method.
Vector Config
sources:
  haproxy_logs:
    type: journald
    include_units:
      - haproxy
transforms:
  extract_haproxy:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - haproxy_logs
      source: |
        . = parse_syslog!(.message)
        del(.appname)
        del(.facility)
        del(.hostname)
        del(.msgid)
        del(.procid)
        del(.severity)
        del(.version)

        .http_request = .request.uri
        .http_status_code = .response.status_code
        .http_verb = .request.method

title: Looking for advice on high latency networks
bodyText:
Question
Our Vector pipeline reads events from Kafka and publishes to an AWS Kinesis Stream with plenty of shards. We are experiencing back pressure in the form of Kafka consumer lag on high latency networks:

ping latency of 20-70ms
vector_adaptive_concurrency_observed_rtt_bucket of 125-250ms
vector_adaptive_concurrency_limit_bucket of 8-32
vector cpu usage 20-25% per thread, total 200%

We have also tested a static concurrency of 64 to 8192 with no improvement.
Do you have any advice or guidance for performance tuning on high latency networks?
P.S. I have read through an existing discussion but figured I would post our specific scenario and question.

    type: "remap"
    inputs:

    source: |

title: how does the lifecycle: preStop work in the vectordotdev Helm chart
bodyText:
Question
I am deploying Vector on EKS using the Helm chart:
https://github.com/vectordotdev/helm-charts/blob/develop/charts/vector/values.yaml
I am running Vector on Spot instances in EKS. Since AWS can terminate Spot instances at any time, I want to configure a lifecycle.preStop hook in values.yaml so that Vector has 120 seconds to flush its buffers before the Pod is terminated.
I have also configured:
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
However, no matter how I configure lifecycle.preStop, I always see the following error events:
kubectl get events -n webcloud-vector --watch | grep PreStopHook
32s         Warning   FailedPreStopHook   pod/vector-5bc8fbfc4-m6ncm   PreStopHook failed
4m15s       Warning   FailedPreStopHook   pod/vector-6b978b946f-7kzrd   PreStopHook failed
100s        Warning   FailedPreStopHook   pod/vector-6b978b946f-kznl2   PreStopHook failed
2m18s       Warning   FailedPreStopHook   pod/vector-6b978b946f-rrzdq   PreStopHook failed

When Vector receives the SIGTERM signal, I see the following logs, but I do not see any logs related to the lifecycle.preStop hook. This is confusing to me, and I am not fully sure how the lifecycle hook works in this case.
[appconfig agent] 2026/01/19 17:56:12 INFO shutdown complete (actual duration: 50ms)
2026-01-19T17:56:13.037001Z  INFO vector::signal: Signal received. signal="SIGTERM"
2026-01-19T17:56:13.037035Z  INFO vector: Vector has stopped.
2026-01-19T17:56:13.038336Z  INFO vector::topology::running: Shutting down... Waiting on running components. remaining_components="parse_syslog_raw, syslog_udp, print_syslog" time_remaining="59 seconds left"
[2026-01-19 17:56:33] Fetching config from AppConfig Agent...

When Vector receives SIGTERM, what exactly does Vector do at that point?
The log shows time_remaining="59 seconds left". Can this shutdown time be configured to be longer?
So My questions are:

How to setup  and config preSop in the value.yaml
When the vector receive SIGTERM, what can we do to flush all the buffer?
What is time_remaining="59 seconds left means,  can we increase this time_remaining, i cannot find any setting regarding this ?

### Vector Config

lifecycle:
  preStop:
     exec:
        command:
         - /bin/sleep
         - "10"



# Startup probe - gives Vector time to load configs before readiness/liveness checks
# This prevents crashes during initial config loading
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health

title: [Q&A] How to handle year boundary with parsing timestamp.
bodyText:
Question
Description
When parsing timestamps for logs that don't include year information, there's a problem with year extraction at year boundaries, causing log insertion failures.
is there a way to specify timezone when using now() or when parsing timestamps?
(without changing the timestamp format of the original log)
Log timestamp examples

ncdn: Nov  7 12:14:05.941 ...
dns: Jan  5 14:45:39

Problem

VictoriaLogs supports ISO8601/RFC3339 or unix timestamp formats
Therefore, Jan  5 14:45:39 needs to be converted to RFC3339 format with year information
At year boundaries, incorrect year values are extracted, causing log insertion failures

Root Cause

now() returns UTC time, but the actual logs are in KST (UTC+9)
During the period from 00:00 to 09:00 KST on January 1st, UTC time is still December 31st of the previous year
This causes the year to be set to the previous year, resulting in timestamps that are too old and failing VictoriaLogs retention period validation

Vector Config
# timestamp conversion (Oct 28 17:27:46)
.year = format_timestamp!(now(), "%Y") # now() returns UTC time year
.log_timestamp = to_string(.year) + " " + to_string!(.logdate) # When combining this way, during +09:00Z 2026/01/01 00:00 ~ 09:00, year value returns 2025, which converts to 2024 when converted +09:00Z.
.timestamp, err = parse_timestamp(.log_timestamp, format: "%Y %b %d %H:%M:%S")
if err != null {
  log(err, level: "error")
}

title: Preventing One Noisy Pod from Overloading kubernetes_logs Source in Vector
bodyText:
Our Setup
We run pods from different services on the same Kubernetes node and use a Vector daemon pod on the node to collect logs using the kubernetes_logs source, apply some transformation, and eventually send to the datadog_logs sink.
The Problem
If one service was buggy and generated a large volume of logs, we observed that the kubernetes_logs source could consume excessive memory, leading to an OOM.
We are looking for a way to achieve "fair sharing" or "resource isolation" so that a single misbehaving service does not impact the log collection of other colocated pods.
What We Have Tried


We have tried using the throttling filter, which can enforce rate limits per pod or per namespace. However, since the throttling filter is applied downstream of the kubernetes_logs source, it doesn't prevent the source from processing the buggy pod's logs at a high speed (and consuming a lot of memory). In fact, because the throttling filter discards messages quickly, it doesn't create backpressure for kubernetes_logs, causing it to process logs even faster compared to when backpressure is applied by the datadog_logs sink.
If kubernetes_logs itself provided a configuration option to limit the rate of log lines read from each k8s pod or namespace, it would satisfy our use case. However, such a configuration option doesn’t seem to exist.


We have also tried using the request.rate_limit_num setting of the datadog_logs sink. It successfully creates backpressure to the kubernetes_logs source and causes it to slow down processing incoming logs, preventing the excessive memory consumption. But this approach does not provide fair sharing, meaning logs from the normal pods are also blocked when the rate limit is reached.


Related issues
#17123 Limit memory usage for sources - Make vector 'resource aware': If this issue is resolved, it would help prevent our Vector daemon from OOMing. However, in addition to that, we also want to enforce "fair sharing", which remains unsolved by the solutions proposed in that issue.

title: How to monitor the number of lines in logs per minute?
bodyText:
Question
Hi all,
I want to start using Vector. For the first thing I decided to monitor the number of log lines per minute (as a proxy for the general server activity – the idea is that if it drops or goes up suddenly, it most probably means trouble, like a DoS attack or unexpected downtime). Since my app is managed by pm2, this means pm2 logs. (This means I just want to know how many new lines appear in /home/me/.pm2/logs/my-app-out.log every minute.) With some help from an LLM, I came up with the following vector.toml (below).
Now I have two questions about it.

Is it a good approach? I have a gut feeling that it might be a bit overengineered – ~50 SLOC for a seemingly simple task.
Much more importantly, when I look in my database, it turns out that the events with the amount of log lines "per minute" are not really inserted once per minute. On average, they seem to be (more or less), but sometimes I get two rows in 30 seconds and sometimes no row for 90 seconds. I noticed that the distribution is fairly uniform (one row every ~60 seconds) when the load on the app is uniform, too (either very low or very high). What can be the reason?

Vector Config
[sources.real_logs]
type = "file"
include = ["/home/me/.pm2/logs/my-app-out.log"]
read_from = "end"

# Artificial events so that something will be recorded even in
# intervals with no log lines.
[sources.heartbeat]
type = "demo_logs"
format = "json"
interval = 30.0

# Wipe all data (. = {}) to ensure both events look identical (same
# tags) so they fall into the same aggregation bucket.
[transforms.normalize_counts]
type = "remap"
inputs = ["real_logs", "heartbeat"]
source = '''
  # Check if it came from a file before we wipe the data
  is_real_log = exists(.file)

  # Save the original timestamp
  ts = .timestamp

  # WIPE EVERYTHING. Removes random fields from demo_logs and file paths.
  . = {}

  # Restore the timestamp
  .timestamp = ts

  # Set the value: 1 for real logs, 0 for heartbeats
  .amount = if is_real_log { 1 } else { 0 }
'''

[transforms.count_lines]
type = "log_to_metric"
inputs = ["normalize_counts"]

  [[transforms.count_lines.metrics]]
  type = "counter"
  field = "amount"
  name = "pm2_logs_account"

  # IMPORTANT: This tells Vector to read the number (0 or 1)
  # instead of just counting +1 because the field exists.
  increment_by_value = true

[transforms.sum_per_minute]
type = "aggregate"
inputs = ["count_lines"]
# 60000ms = 1 minute
interval_ms = 60000

# This is needed because the `adapt_to_schema` transform would not
# work on metric events.
[transforms.metric_to_log]
type = "metric_to_log"
inputs = ["sum_per_minute"]

[transforms.adapt_to_schema]
type = "remap"
inputs = ["metric_to_log"]
source = '''
  .server = get_env_var("HOSTNAME") ?? "unknown"
  .value = .counter.value
  del(.kind)
  del(.counter)
'''

[sinks.database]
type = "postgres"
inputs = ["adapt_to_schema"]
endpoint = "[REDACTED]"
table = "[REDACTED]"

[sinks.console]
type = "console"
inputs = ["sum_per_minute"]
target = "stdout" 

  [sinks.console.encoding]
  codec = "json" # Outputs clear JSON structure

title: How to realize a sequence count on message (stream) - focus for auditing?

Question
Hello everybody,
we are currently integrating vector as a cool logging filter for dedicated purposes - in our case focus for "audit-logs".
So we need some (simple) solution for the questions:

Has somebody edited the audit.log file? (e.g. with an editor removed lines)
Are there audit-messages lost, e.g. as feeding to a cloud service? (e.g. in the network transfer)

One simple solution were a sequence count...

Potential solutions


I could imagine to solve this question with a dedicated (new) transform, which has the only purpose to generate a sequence count. The counter state could then be stored within the context, and survive also a vector restart to be continued without interruption.


Alternatively, if one could syntactically access "per message" the metrics of the remap transform for the counter component_received_events_total via vrl, the issue could be solved that way. Unfortunately I am not aware of this kind of access.

title: Cuckoo filter + LRU - seems like a natural match for Vector?
bodyText:
We need memory-efficient, CPU-efficient ways of caching large numbers of event keys so that we do not re-transmit the same things more than once (ideally.)  However, as mentioned, we have limited memory so we'd like to evict things that aren't recently hot. A Cuckoo filter would be the ideal candidate (it supports deletions, unlike Bloom) but what we really need is Cuckoo + LRU eviction. Any suggestions for a Cuckoo Rust library for starters?  I see only one paper on Cuckoo + LRU, and no Rust code for it, and really I see only one Rust Cuckoo implementation.
I don't know how many bits would have to be added to each object for an LRU timer, but it would seem to me that this could be done very efficiently with just a few bits if you divide the memory space into "buckets" and just evict all the members of a  bucket when capacity is reached instead of keeping timers/counts. You'd only need the number of bits in each object to match the bucket size. 5 bits, 32 buckets, etc.   I'm sure someone more clever has reduced this even more significantly.
We would be open to developing this feature (and probably will) but guidance on easier/better paths is welcome.
Counter-point: we could just use a hash + LRU model, but that doesn't seem to be quite as memory-efficient as Cuckoo.
References:
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10489-021-02567-0
https://github.com/axiomhq/rust-cuckoofilter
https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~dga/papers/cuckoo-conext2014.pdf

title: Understanding datadog_agent source internal metrics and logs
bodyText:
Question
Hi vector team and everyone,
May I check and learn more about the internal metrics and logs related to datadog_agent source (ref).
A small context is that I've just recently rolled out the Vector to receive and handle a large amount of metrics traffic from the internal datadog agents (configuring using the observability_pipelines_worker option).
I've also configured quite an extensive dashboards to monitor vector and noticed periodic metric data of  component_discarded_events_total with intentional tag/label as false (ref). Usually accompanying by:

an internal ERROR log of Events dropped at datadog_agent source
some internal WARN logs of HTTP error and Retrying after error (with some suppressions) at datadog_metrics sink
memory buffer and usage increased expectedly
sometimes Adaptive Concurrency RTT gets worse/spiked as well

So I'm trying to understand what was the real reason of the Events dropped issue in this case. In documentation, it just mentions there's due to errors but is it errors from Vector Sink or is it from the Source Datadog Agents in this case? Metrics Events dropped means all the data is permanently lost because I don't enable acknowledgement feature? Any recommendations to mitigate or avoid this issue?
I put some of the most important configurations below to avoid too much configs. Generally, I don't see any errors or discarded events at the transforms stage thus I remove it from this context to avoid noise.
Thank you for spending the time, I know this is a lot of context.
Vector Config
There are many context for the below configs though I'm open for recommendations:

An average metric event size in our system is 4-5KB thus I have to decrease the max batch events to improve RTT from Datadog API Endpoint. If keeping the default size, it would take >30s and surely dropped along the way.
Memory events buffer also is being used the maximum usually go up to 70-80% with this 400,000 events config
Concurrency settings I tried to make it scale out as fast and as many as possible since this is Datadog Platform. They don't limit metrics submissions in their endpoint (ref). But this doesn't prevent 500 error msg returned sometimes and decrease concurrency (though back up quite fast).
Also due to the above reasons, I decrease max backoff durations.

sources:

    type: datadog_agent
    address: 0.0.0.0:9000
    disable_logs: true
    disable_traces: true

    inputs:
      - datadog_agents
    type: datadog_metrics
    default_api_key: "${DD_API_KEY:?missing DD_API_KEY as default}"

      - type: memory

        when_full: block

      adaptive_concurrency: 
        initial_concurrency: 600
        max_concurrency_limit: 1500
        decrease_ratio: 1.0
        rtt_deviation_scale: 3.0
        ewma_alpha: 0.4

title: Manual rules/remaps for batching/buffering?
bodyText:
Question
Hello!
Vector's default implementation for opentelmetry/http sinks automatically batches JSON records into JSON array, which doesn't seem to be correct OTLP protocol. The best I could do is disable framing completely and limit max events per send to 1. Is it possible to somehow specify how batching should be performed? Or maybe there are some examples how to do manual batching via "reduce" transformer? The best I can guess is to remap events, then reduce them, then remap again into OTLP payload, then send via raw HTTP.
Thanks
P.S: Two VRL files mentioned in remap serve to first transform Rust's tracing JSON logs into more convenient form and then transform that form into OTLP payloads. Adding them just for completeness, though they don't affect question directly
Vector Config
config.yaml:
sources:
  backend_logs:
    type: file
    include: ["backend.log"]
    # Used for debug only
    ignore_checkpoints: true

transforms:
  backend_service_name:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - backend_logs
    source: |
      .service_name = "backend"
  backend_remap:
    type: remap
    inputs:
      - backend_service_name
    files:
      - rust-logs.vrl
      - otlp-payload.vrl

sinks:
  backend_openobserve:
    type: http
    inputs:
      - backend_remap
    uri: "https://api.eu1.honeycomb.io/v1/logs"
    method: post
    encoding:
      codec: json
    headers:
      Content-Type: "application/json"
      X-Honeycomb-Team: <API key>
      X-Honeycomb-Dataset: "backend"
    batch:
      max_events: 1
      timeout_secs: 1
    framing:
      method: bytes
    request:
      timeout_secs: 30  # backend_openobserve:
rust-logs.vrl
# Converts Rust's tracing JSON output into format ingestible by OTLP payload former

tstamp = ""
message = ""
level = "INFO"
service_name = null
attributes = {}

# Keep service name if it was assigned before parsing
if is_string(.service_name) {
    service_name = .service_name
}

# Parse JSON message first (if needed)
if is_string(.message) {
    . = parse_json!(string!(.message))
}

# Fetch timestamp from JSON, it's mandatory
tstamp = .timestamp

# Handle message. It's either on top level or inside "fields"

if exists(.message) {
    message = to_string!(.message)
}

# Flatten "fields" into attributes - except `.fields.message` which replaces global message

if exists(.fields) && is_object(.fields) {
    if exists(.fields.message) {
        message = to_string!(.fields.message)
        del(.fields.message)
    }
    # Merge all fields from .fields into "attributes"
    attributes = merge!(attributes, .fields)
}

# Process spans - collect from "span" object and "spans" array
spans_to_process = []

# Collect span from "span" object field
if exists(.span) && is_object(.span) {
    spans_to_process = push(spans_to_process, .span)
}

# Collect spans from "spans" array field
if exists(.spans) && is_array(.spans) {
    for_each(array!(.spans)) -> |_index, span_item| {
        if is_object(span_item) {
            spans_to_process = push(spans_to_process, span_item)
        }
    }
}

# Process each collected span
for_each(spans_to_process) -> |_index, span_obj| {
    # Get span name (default to "unknown" if missing)
    span_name = get(span_obj, ["name"]) ?? "unknown"
    
    # Process each field in the span object
    for_each(object!(span_obj)) -> |field_name, field_value| {
        # Skip the "name" field since we use it as prefix
        if field_name != "name" {
            # Create field name: {span_name}_{field_name}
            new_field_name = join!([span_name, field_name], "_")
            # Assign to root object
            attributes = set!(attributes, [new_field_name], field_value)
        }
    }
}

# 3. Rename code location fields
if exists(.target) {
    attributes.code_target = .target
}

if exists(.filename) {
    attributes.code_file = .filename
}

if exists(.line_number) {
    attributes.code_line = .line_number
}

# Form and return final object
. = {
    "timestamp": tstamp,
    "message": message,
    "level": level,
    "attributes": attributes
}

if is_string(service_name) {
    .service_name = service_name
}

.

otlp-payload.vrl:
# This VRL expects following incoming JSON format:
# * `timestamp` - timestamp in `%Y-%M-%DT%h:%m:%s.%ms%Z` format
# * `message` - log message, goes into body
# * `level` - log level, `ERROR`/`WARN`/`INFO`/`DEBUG`/`TRACE`
# * `service_name` - goes into resource.attributes."service.name" if present
# * `attributes` - object with event's custom attributes; all are stringified ATM

# OTLP's severity table
otlp_severity = {
  "TRACE": 1,
  "TRACE2": 2,
  "TRACE3": 3,
  "TRACE4": 4,
  "DEBUG": 5,
  "DEBUG2": 6,
  "DEBUG3": 7,
  "DEBUG4": 8,
  "INFO": 9,
  "INFO2": 10,
  "INFO3": 11,
  "INFO4": 12,
  "WARN": 13,
  "WARN2": 14,
  "WARN3": 15,
  "WARN4": 16,
  "ERROR": 17,
  "ERROR2": 18,
  "ERROR3": 19,
  "ERROR4": 20,
  "FATAL": 21,
  "FATAL2": 22,
  "FATAL3": 23,
  "FATAL4": 24,
}

# Severity text and number from level
# Default level is info
severity_text = "INFO"
severity_number = 9

if exists(.level) {
    severity_text = string!(.level)

    level_num, err = get(otlp_severity, [severity_text])
    # Keep unknown levels at "INFO"
    if err == null {
        severity_number = level_num
    }
}

# Compose attributes into OTEL format
attributes = []

for_each(object!(.attributes)) -> |field_name, field_value| {
    attributes = push(attributes, {
        "key": field_name,
        "value": { "stringValue": to_string!(field_value) }
    })
}

tstamp = parse_timestamp!(.timestamp, "%+")

# Compose final event
event = {
    "scopeLogs": [{
        "logRecords": [{
            "timeUnixNano": to_unix_timestamp!(tstamp, unit: "nanoseconds"),
            "body": { "stringValue": string!(.message) },
            "severityText": severity_text,
            "severityNumber": severity_number,
            "attributes": attributes
        }]
    }]
}

# Add service name if set
if exists(.service_name) && is_string(.service_name) {
    event.resource = {
        "attributes": [
            { "key": "service.name", "value": { "stringValue": .service_name } },
        ]
    }
}

. = {
    "resourceLogs": [event]
}

.

title: How to correctly aggregate metrics when dropping host tag?
bodyText:
Question
I am currently building a Datadog Agent -> Vector -> Datadog API pipeline to drop the host tag before it is sent to Datadog. The motivation behind this is to reduce cardinality and thereby costs. I understand that dropping the host tag imposes the risk of data point duplication in Datadog, which would result in duplicate points of the same time series overwriting original points.
In order to prevent this issue, I am using an aggregation transform to consolidate data points within Vector after the host tag has been dropped. This seems like it should work without incurring any data loss, but the filtered/aggregated metrics are consistently lower than the original metrics with the host tag. I have attached a screenshot of the test metrics.
blue: original metrics, purple: removing host with aggregation, yellow: removing host without aggregation

I would appreciate any guidance on how to aggregate these metrics such that they are accurate despite removing the host tag. Thank you!
Vector Config
# Sources - receive data from Datadog agents
    sources:
      datadog_agents:
        type: datadog_agent
        address: 0.0.0.0:8282
        multiple_outputs: true
        store_api_key: false
        
 # Transforms - delete unnecessary host tags (cardinality reduction)
    transforms:
      remove_host_tag:
        type: remap
        inputs:
          - datadog_agents.metrics
        source: |-
          # Add missing cluster tags using the same logic as datadog-agent.yaml lines 72-83
          # These should come from DD_TAGS but don't due to agent bug: https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/issues/15128

          log("RAW DATA RECEIVED: " + encode_json(.))

          cluster_env = "${CLUSTER_APP_ENVIRONMENT}"
          cluster_group = "${CLUSTER_APP_GROUP}"
          cluster_name = "${CLUSTER_NAME}"
          cluster_region = "${CLUSTER_REGION}"

          if cluster_env != "" {
            .tags.env = cluster_env
          }
          if cluster_group != "" {
            .tags.app_group = cluster_group
          }
          if cluster_name != "" {
            .tags.eks_cluster = cluster_name
            .tags.cluster_name = cluster_name
            .tags.cluster_id = cluster_name
          }
          if cluster_region != "" {
            .tags.region = cluster_region
          }

          if (exists(.tags.host) && exists(.tags.remove_host_tag)) {
            host_value = .tags.host
            del(.tags.host)
            # If the metric is not a distribution, we need to set a tag for uniqueness. Use the vector host, which should have lower cardinality than the datadog host.
            if .kind != "distribution" {
              .tags.vector_host = "${HOSTNAME}"
            }
          }

          # log("UPDATED TAGS: " + encode_json(.tags))

      consolidate_metrics:
          type: aggregate
          inputs:
            - remove_host_tag

# Sinks - forward processed data to Datadog
    sinks:
      datadog_metrics:
        type: datadog_metrics
        inputs:
          - consolidate_metrics
        default_api_key: "${DATADOG_API_KEY}"
        site: "us5.datadoghq.com"

title: vector gauge to distribution aggregation mode
bodyText:
Question
Hello,
Problem Statement
Currently, Vector emits individual metric events, which can result in high event volumes, especially in high-cardinality environments. This impacts:

Network bandwidth and storage costs
Downstream system performance
Processing overhead in analytics pipelines

Proposed Solution
Add a new Distribution aggregation mode to the aggregate transform that:

Collects multiple absolute metrics with the same series (name, tags, etc.) during a flush interval.
Aggregates them into a single Distribution metric containing all individual values as samples.
Ignores incremental metrics (counters) to maintain their semantic meaning.
Reduces payload count while increasing payload density.

Benefits

Volume Reduction: N individual metrics → 1 distribution metric per series
Preserved Accuracy: All original values retained as distribution samples
Downstream Flexibility: Analytics databases can convert to histograms at query time
Cost Optimisation: Lower network/storage costs due to reduced event count

Use Cases

Time-series databases that support native distribution types (e.g., ClickHouse, InfluxDB)
Analytics workflows requiring statistical analysis across measurement windows
High-cardinality metrics where overall event volume reduction is critical
Cost-sensitive environments where network/storage efficiency matters

Example
Before (3 separate events):
gauge_cpu_usage{host="web01"} 45.2
gauge_cpu_usage{host="web01"} 47.1  
gauge_cpu_usage{host="web01"} 44.8

After (1 distribution event):
gauge_cpu_usage{host="web01"} distribution{samples: [45.2, 47.1, 44.8]}

This approach is particularly well-suited for analytics databases that can convert distributions into equal-width histogram buckets or other aggregations at query time, providing flexibility for various downstream use cases.
We can contribute to this, but as the contribution guidelines mention, I wanted to raise the question of seeking collaboration before coding the solution.
Thanks in advance.
Vector Config
Using the existing TOML example with the proposed mode distribution.
[transforms.my_transform_id]
type = "aggregate"
inputs = [ "my-source-or-transform-id" ]
interval_ms = 10_000
mode = "distribution"

title: Dedupe per "source scrape"
bodyText:
Question
Hello,
The title is not very clear but let me explain my pipeline. I have a HTTP endpoint that return a JSON where one of the value is "syslog" content as a string. I then have the following transform that split the syslog string as multiple events:
daemon_extract_log:
   type: "remap"
   inputs: ["daemon"]

   source: |
     fetch_timestamp = now()

     parsed = parse_json!(.message)
     lines = split!(parsed.data, "\n")

     . = map_values(lines) -> |value| {
       {
         "source_file": "daemon_debug.log",
         "ip": "X.X.X.X",
         "mac": "XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX",
         "fetch_timestamp": fetch_timestamp,
         "message": value
       }
     }
Down the pipeline, I have another transform that parse each syslog line:
  parse_process_log:
    type: "remap"
    inputs: ["routing.process"]
    drop_on_error: true
    source: |
      . |= parse_regex!(.message, r'^\[(?P<timestamp>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2})\] \[(?P<severity>\w+)\] (?P<process>\w+)\[(?P<pid>\d+)\]: (?P<message>.+)$')

      # Coerce parsed fields
      .timestamp = parse_timestamp!(.timestamp, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
      .pid = to_int!(.pid)
      .message = strip_whitespace(.message)
I need to dedupe my logs but the issue is I might have syslog lines like this:
[2025-09-17 19:05:32] [WARNING] lanbrowser[971]: [pub] no host to reclaim: list is full with persistent and reachable hosts
[2025-09-17 19:05:32] [WARNING] lanbrowser[971]: [pub] no host to reclaim: list is full with persistent and reachable hosts
[2025-09-17 19:05:35] [WARNING] lanbrowser[971]: [pub] no host to reclaim: list is full with persistent and reachable hosts
[2025-09-17 19:05:35] [WARNING] lanbrowser[971]: [pub] no host to reclaim: list is full with persistent and reachable hosts

I want to keep all those lines the first time I scraped them, but not the following times. The issue is that for Vector, it can't differentiate the events that comes from the first scrape from the events that comes from the following scrapes.
I currently have a external dedupe that does the following post-Vector but I would love to be able to integrate its functionality inside Vector:
def dedupe_logs(input_path, key_fields=("timestamp", "message",)):
    seen = {}
    deduped = []
    with open(input_path, "r") as file:
        for line in file:
            log = json.loads(line)
            key = tuple(log[field] for field in key_fields)
            fetch_timestamp = log["fetch_timestamp"]

            if key not in seen:
                seen[key] = fetch_timestamp
            else:
                if seen[key] != fetch_timestamp:
                    continue
            deduped.append(log)
    return deduped
If VRL was stafeful, I could manage to do something, but it's not.
Do you have an idea that could help me?
Vector Config
No response

title: error=Missing environment variable in config. name = "date"
bodyText:
Question
./vector --version
vector 0.49.0
run
2025-09-19T06:01:28.155759Z ERROR vector::cli: Configuration error. error=Missing environment variable in config. name = "date"
Vector Config
[sources.abc]
type = "file"
include = ["/a.log"]
data_dir = "/abc"


[transforms.parse_outer]
type = "remap"
inputs = ["abc"]
source = '''
.log_file = .file
parsed, err = parse_json(.message)

if err == null {
  .timestamp1 = parsed.t["$date"]
  .severity = parsed.s
  .component = parsed.c
  .id = parsed.id
  .context = parsed.ctx
  .msg = parsed.msg

  if is_object(parsed.attr) {
    .attr_mechanism = parsed.attr.mechanism
    .attr_speculative = parsed.attr.speculative
    .attr_principalName = parsed.attr.principalName
    .attr_authenticationDatabase = parsed.attr.authenticationDatabase
    .attr_remote = parsed.attr.remote
    .attr_extraInfo = parsed.attr.extraInfo
  }
